blocks.text: Time Complexity of the Optimized Algorithm
Let's look at how fast our algorithm works after making two improvements.
First, finding the starting node (the prefix node) takes a very short time, noted as O(1).
Second, getting the top k queries is also very quick because we save those results, which is also O(1).
Because both steps now take O(1) time, our whole algorithm only needs O(1) to get the top k queries.
In our earlier design, every time you typed a search word, we updated the data right away.
However, this method has two major problems.
First, users can search billions of times each day. This constant updating can slow down how quickly we respond to queries.
Second, once we create the data structure (the trie) for suggestions, the top choices don't change very often. So, we don’t need to update the trie all the time.
To create a data gathering service that can grow, we need to understand where the data comes from and how it will be used.
For real-time services like Twitter, we need fresh suggestions immediately.
But for many Google searches, the top suggestions usually stay the same daily.
Even though the needs are different, the basic idea behind the data gathering service stays the same.
The information we use to build the trie generally comes from analyzing user behavior or tracking usage (analytics or logging services).
The redesigned data gathering service is illustrated in Figure 13-9, and we will review each part step by step.

script:
With improvements, query retrieval times can drastically decrease. Finding the starting node now takes O(1) time. That’s a constant time. Getting those top k query suggestions also takes O(1) because we save those results ahead of time. This means that both steps together also need O(1) time. It’s efficient. Our entire algorithm now performs in O(1) time to get the top k queries.

The benefits of these improvements are huge. First, users get faster responses. When you type something, those quick suggestions pop up right away. This makes the search experience smoother and more enjoyable. The system can handle a lot of users without slowing down. So, less lag equals happier users. It’s that straightforward. Understanding how these changes affect times sets the stage for robust data structures in future discussions.
